newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - July 10.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - July 10.

text.p: THE DOMINION

Super 'no' won't kill tax cuts says Birch: Tax cuts over the next five years would remain a government priority even if voters opposed the compulsory retirement savings scheme in September's referendum, Finance Minister Bill Birch said on Wednesday. Page 1.

Gene-altered food imports 'can't be identified': The Ministry of Health has no way of knowing which imported food products contain genetically modified material, a parliamentary select committee was told on Wednesday. Page 1.

Moratorium on casinos difficult says control body: Imposing a moratorium on new casinos until after the government had passed a law on gambling would cause more problems than MPs realised, Casino Control Authority chairman Jock Irvine said on Wednesday. Page 2.

Education Ministry criticised for neglecting Maori needs: The Education Ministry has been criticised in a report issued on Wednesday by Te Puni Kokiri (the Maori Development Ministry) as failing to tackle the poor education results of Maoris. Page 2.
Engineers to study Beehive shift idea: The government may know by the end of this month whether it is feasible to move the Beehive to make way for the completion of Parliament Buildings. Page 2.

Tax credit reform 'overlooked': Last week's announcement of a tax credit for superannuation savers on lower tax rates was the most important tax reform proposal since gst, but was overshadowed by the compulsory superannuation debate, FPG Research managing director Graham Rich said on Wednesday. Page 15.
THE NEW ZEALAND HERALD

Treasurer fuels dollar slide: A seemingly casual remark by the Treasurer, Winston Peters, sent the New Zealand dollar diving on Wednesday and prompted fears of more nervous overnight selling in world markets.
Starting date will vary pension level: A "yes" vote in the superannuation referendum will mean that some retired New Zealanders will be paid bigger pensions than others.
Red ink leaves Sky untroubled: Sky Network Television insists it is in sound financial heart, despite recording a $20.6 million loss last year.

Rivals join together to chase business in water industry: Anglian Water of Britain and United States-controlled Waste Management are putting aside some of their rivalry to jointly pursue business in the New Zealand water industry.

Courts Dept seeks new powers: The Department of Courts, which has just been given approval to spend $100 million on information systems over the next three years, wants legislative power to collect fines earlier and to perform data-matching to catch defaulters.
Foresters join MAF shake-up: Forest owners will work closely with the government in the establishment of the new merged Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry, despite their opposition to the move.

Crown case 'relies on conspiracy': The Crown's fraud case against former Pacer Kerridge executive chairman David Phillips relied on a massive and unlikely conspiracy, defence counsel Gary Judd QC, said on Wednesday.
THE PRESS

Lake Alice abuse claims horrify Minister: Health Minister Bill English said on Wednesday he had been horrified by the allegations of abuse by former Lake Alice Hospital patients and had no reason to disbelieve their stories. Page 3.

MP unhelpful about Morgan's diary, police say: The police diplomatic protection squad at Parliament said on Wednesday an opposition MP it was speaking to about the disappearance of NZ First MP Tuku Morgan's diary was not being helpful. Page 3.

Michael Hill tills ring the same: Michael Hill International, which runs jewellery stores in Australia and New Zealand says sales were flat in the first six months of 1997 and competition has crimped any gains from the lower gold price. Page 35.
